'''John Todd''' (born 1939) is a Canadian [[biologist]] working in the general field of [[ecological design]]. 
He addresses problems of [[food production]] and [[wastewater]] processing by using ecosystems technologies that incorporate plants, animals and bacteria.<ref name="Lindbergh"/>  Todd has developed "Arks" or "bioshelters",<ref name="Distillations"/> ecologically closed "life-support systems"<ref name="Distillations"/> with the goal of sustainable functioning. He combines [[alternative technology|alternative technologies]] for [[renewable energy]], [[organic farming]], [[aquaculture]], [[hydroponics]] and [[architecture]]<ref name="Distillations">{{cite journal|last1=  Eardley-Pryor |first1=Roger |title=Love, Peace, and Technoscience |journal=Distillations |date=2017|volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=38–41 |url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/love-peace-and-technoscience }}</ref> to create "living machines"<ref name="Laylin"/><ref name="Kaiser">{{cite book|editor-last1=Kaiser|editor-first1=David|editor-last2=McCray|editor-first2=W. Patrick|first=Henry|last= Trim|chapter=A Quest for Permanence: The Ecological Visioneering of John Todd and the New Alchemy Institute|title=Groovy Science: Knowledge, Innovation, and American Counterculture|date=2016|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-37291-4}}</ref><ref name="Wells">{{cite journal|last1=Todd|first1=John|last2=Brown|first2=Erica J.G|last3=Wells|first3=Erik|title=Ecological design applied|journal=Ecological Engineering|date=October 2003|volume=20|issue=5|pages=421–440|doi=10.1016/j.ecoleng.2003.08.004|url=https://ewrel.fiu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/EcologicalDesign_Todd-et-al_2003.pdf|access-date=1 May 2018}}</ref>
or "eco-machines".<ref name="Santoro"/>

John Todd is a co-founder with [[Nancy Jack Todd]] of the non-profits [[New Alchemy Institute]] (1969–1991)<ref name="SA">{{cite web|title=New Alchemy Institute Institution – Cape Cod, USA 1969 – 1991|url=http://www.spatialagency.net/database/why/ecological/new.alchemy.institute|website=Spatial Agency|access-date=1 May 2018}}</ref> and [[Ocean Arks International]] (1981),<ref>{{cite web|title=Nancy Jack Todd|url=https://www.bfi.org/challenge/about/selection-process/advisory-team/nancy-jack-todd|access-date=26 April 2018|website=Buckminster Fuller Institute|archive-date=27 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180427120105/https://www.bfi.org/challenge/about/selection-process/advisory-team/nancy-jack-todd|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Hannum">{{cite web|last1=Hannum|first1=Hildegarde|title=Introduction|url=http://www.centerforneweconomics.org/publications/lectures/todd/nancy-jack/the-promise-of-ecological-design|website=Schumacher Center for a New Economics|access-date=26 April 2018}}</ref><ref name="Lerner">{{cite book|last1=Lerner|first1=Steve|title=Eco-pioneers : practical visionaries solving today's environmental problems|date=2005|publisher=MIT Press|location=Cambridge, Mass.|isbn=9780262621243|pages=47–66|chapter=John Todd: Greenhouse treatment of municipal sewage|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XCUXig07qcgC&pg=PA47|access-date=2 May 2018}}</ref>
and the founder and president of the design and engineering firm John Todd Ecological Design Inc. (1989).<ref>{{cite web|title=Who we are|url=http://www.toddecological.com/index.php?id=about|website=John Todd Ecological Design Inc.|access-date=27 April 2018|archive-date=27 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180427120408/http://www.toddecological.com/index.php?id=about|url-status=dead}}</ref>
A research professor emeritus and distinguished lecturer at the [[University of Vermont]],<ref name="Emeritus">{{cite news|title=Ecological engineer John Todd to lecture April 11|url=https://www.skidmore.edu/news/2013/0407-john-todd-to-lecture.php |access-date=1 May 2018|work=Skidmore|date=April 7, 2013}}</ref>
Todd has published books on ecological design, as well as over 200 scientific papers, popular articles and essays.<ref name="Lindbergh"/>

==Early life and education==
Todd was born in [[Hamilton, Ontario|Hamilton]], [[Ontario]], Canada in 1939 and grew up near Hamilton Bay on [[Lake Ontario]].<ref name="Omega">{{cite web|title=Our Fate Hinges on Water Reclamation An Interview With John Todd|url=https://www.eomega.org/article/our-fate-hinges-on-water-reclamation|website=Omega Center for Sustainable Living|date=March 31, 2017}}</ref> The area near his home included marshes and streams which were being badly damaged by pollution. The writings of [[Louis Bromfield]] offered Todd a "marvelous tale of hope" about the possibility of land restoration.<ref name="Brown"/>

Todd earned his B.Sc. (1961) in agriculture and his M.Sc. (1963) in [[parasitology]] and [[tropical medicine]] at [[McGill University]] in [[Montreal]], [[Quebec]], Canada. He then did doctoral work in [[marine biology]] at the [[University of Michigan]], studying [[fisheries]] and [[oceanography]].<ref name="Brown"/><ref name="Wahl"/>  
His early professional interest in the [[behavioral ecology]] of fish was the basis of his work as an assistant professor of [[ethology]] at [[San Diego State University]]<ref name="Brown"/> (1968–1970).<ref name="CV">{{cite web|title=John Todd|url=http://www.uvm.edu/giee/pdfs/JohnToddCV_2008.pdf |website=University of Vermont|access-date=1 May 2018}}</ref>

==Career==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  [[File:Ethel M Living Machine 1.jpg|210px]] |caption= [[Ethel M Chocolate Factory|Ethel M.]] "Living Machine", 2006  | video1 = [https://www.nfb.ca/film/new_alchemists/ “The New Alchemists”], 1974 documentary, Dorothy Todd Hénaut, [[National Film Board of Canada]] |video2= [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXmjrEfyl20 Dr. John Todd Ecological Design on Eco Machines], Tao Lee | video3 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LFXMH5ZbNK8 The Ecological Design Revolution], John Todd, Bioneers | video4= [https://vimeo.com/6345651 Green Eco-Machine], Kristin Alexander }}

John Todd joined the [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]] in [[Woods Hole, Massachusetts]], as an assistant scientist in 1970.<ref name="Chu">{{cite news|last1=Chu|first1=Dan|last2=Brown|first2=S. Avery|title=If You Leave It to Mother Nature, Says Biologist John Todd, Sewage Doesn't Have to Go to Waste|url=http://people.com/archive/if-you-leave-it-to-mother-nature-says-biologist-john-todd-sewage-doesnt-have-to-go-to-waste-vol-32-no-22/|access-date=6 May 2018|work=People|date=November 27, 1989}}</ref><ref name="Brown" /><ref name="Picard" />
At Woods Hole, John Todd began to develop his ideas about how complicated biological food chains worked. 
An important influence on Todd's thinking was his wife, Nancy Jack Todd, a dancer, writer, editor and activist.  In their conversations Nancy wondered if ecological concepts could be applied to address people's needs. She encouraged John Todd to put "a human face" on his research.<ref name="Picard">{{cite news|last1=Picard|first1=Ken|title=A Fuller World View|url=https://www.sevendaysvt.com/vermont/a-fuller-world-view/Content?oid=2134376|access-date=30 April 2018|work=Seven Days|date=July 23, 2008}}</ref><ref name="Brown" />   
Since then, the couple have edited and co-written several books, and are co-recipients of a number of awards.<ref name="Mongillo" />

===New Alchemy Institute===
In 1969 the Todds and William O. McLarney co-founded the [[New Alchemy Institute]] in [[Cape Cod]], [[Massachusetts]]<ref name="Wahl">{{cite web|last1=Wahl|first1=Daniel Christian|title=The New Alchemy Institute: pioneers of ecological design|url=https://medium.com/age-of-awareness/the-new-alchemy-institute-d0992ce33a68|website=Age of Awareness|date=July 12, 2017}}</ref>
to "engage in scientific research in the public interest on  ecologically  and behaviourally planned agriculture systems and rural land based communities."<ref name="Coates"/>{{rp|156}}
The institute was a "fusion of technology and counterculture".<ref name="Coates"/>{{rp|157}}
Its members proposed to apply principles and design strategies from the biological sciences to [[technology]] in ways that would be economically and environmentally sustainable.<ref name="Degrees">{{cite web|title=Dare To Be Naive: New Alchemy Institute|url=http://12degreesoffreedom.org/newalchemyinstitute.html|website=12 degrees of freedom|access-date=1 May 2018}}</ref>  
Although the New Alchemy Institute dissolved in 1991,<ref name="Hugus"/>
it has been described as "a catalyst of change promoting the development of new ecological design solutions, alternative technologies and methods of ecological food production and waste treatment."<ref name="Wahl"/>

One of the approaches they developed was the concept of bioshelters, "greenhouse-like architectural structures containing ecosystems for various purposes: food for humans, waste purification systems, etc."<ref name="Gilman"/>
[[Wendell Berry]] wrote admiringly: "The bioshelter idea, then, proposes to make a household on the pattern of an ecosystem, adapted to the local landscape and climate, using local materials... Its governing principle is symbiosis: the food production system heats the house; the fish tanks raise fish, heat the greenhouse, provide irrigation water and fertilizer for the plants."<ref name="Berry">{{cite book|last1=Berry|first1=Wendell|title=Standing by words : essays|date=2011|publisher=Counterpoint|location=Berkeley|isbn=978-1582437453|page=161|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HbP-DYNu7QUC&pg=PA161|access-date=2 May 2018}}</ref>
The idea that the wastes created in one part of a system provide valuable resources for another part of the system is fundamental to the design of such sustainable ecosystems.<ref name="Laylin"/>

===Ocean Arks International===
In 1981, Todd co-founded the non-profit [[Ocean Arks International]] (OAI).<ref>{{cite web|title=Ocean Arks International|url=http://www.philanthropydirectory.org/charity/ocean-arks-international-inc|website=Catalogue for Philanthropy|access-date=27 April 2018}}</ref><ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|78–79}}
The original idea behind Ocean Arks was to build wind-powered vessels capable of carrying ecological materials and support technologies, for use in countries throughout the developing world. Such a vision was beyond the reach of the organization.<ref name="Gilman"/><ref name="Hunt">{{cite book|last1=Hunt|first1=Sarah|title=DESIGNING ECOSYSTEMS: SYNERGIES AND TENSIONS BETWEEN ENVIRONMENTAL ENTHUSIASMS AND MATERIALITY|date=2010|publisher=The University of Georgia|location=Athens, GA|url=https://getd.libs.uga.edu/pdfs/hunt_sarah_201012_phd.pdf|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref>

Todd began to focus on other concerns relating to water, in particular the development of alternative approaches to conventional waste treatment. He applied ideas from aquaculture and organic agriculture to wastewater. His approach was to identify ecological pathways through which nutrients from waste could be recycled. Waste from one organism could become a food source for subsequent organisms, instead of being discarded as an unusable and toxic by-product.<ref name="Gilman"/><ref name="Hunt"/>

The first "Solar Aquatics System" (SAS) for wastewater treatment was an experimental pilot at the [[Sugarbush Resort|Sugarbush Ski resort]] near [[Warren, Vermont]],<ref name="Hunt"/> around 1986.<ref name="Gilman"/>

During the 1990s, Todd was involved in several attempts to start companies for the technologies he envisioned. The personnel, financing and technologies involved in these companies overlap in complicated and confusing ways, with each other and with Ocean Arks International.<ref name="Hunt"/>   The term "Living Machines" was filed for registration as a [[wordmark]] in 1991, and was registered to Ocean Arks International in 1993 by the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]].<ref name="Hunt"/>

===Ecological Engineering Associates, Inc.===
Ecological Engineering Associates, Inc. (EEA) was founded in [[Marion, Massachusetts]] in 1988 as a commercial venture to more effectively promote the work of [[Ocean Arks International]].<ref name="Gilman">{{cite journal|last1=Gilman|first1=Robert|title=The Restoration Of Waters|journal=Sustainability|date=1990|volume=25|issue=Spring|page=42|url=https://www.context.org/iclib/ic25/todd/|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Reynolds">{{cite news|last1=Reynolds|first1=Larry|title=Munching waste for profit|work=Business Ethics|volume=6|issue=3|page=15|date=1992}}</ref> 
Susan B. Peterson, previously an employee of OAI, became EEA's first president.<ref name="BioCycle">{{cite news|title=Marion, Massachusetts: Treating wastewater with aquatic plants |work=BioCycle |volume=35|date=1994}}</ref>
Co-founder John Todd preferred not to serve on its board, but was involved as an "ecological designer".<ref name="Hunt"/>

EEA designed and installed a wastewater plant to remediate [[septage]] lagoons at [[Harwich, Massachusetts]] (see below). Work began in 1988, and the system became operational in 1990.<ref name="Gilman"/><ref name="Hunt"/>
EEA developed several other projects, using transparent water columns for treatment units in its "solar aquatic systems".<ref name="Hunt"/> 
Patents for processes relating to solar aquatics were filed under the inventor names of John Todd and Barry Silverstein in 1988 and 1991, and granted to EEA.<ref name="Hunt"/><ref name="Patent1992">{{cite web|title=Solar Aquatic Apparatus for Treating Waste, US. Patent 5,087,353, granted February 11 1992|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5087353A/en|website=Google Patents|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Patent1995">{{cite web|title= Method for treating water, US. Patent 5,389,257, granted February 14, 1995|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5389257A/en|website=Google Patents|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref>
EEA registered the trademark "Solar Aquatic" specifically for waste treatment tanks with transparent water columns.<ref name="Josephson">{{cite journal|last1=Todd|first1=John|last2=Josephson|first2=Beth |title=The design of living technologies for waste treatment |journal=Ecological Engineering |date=1996 |volume=6 |issue=1–3|pages=109–136 |url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/06d0/2a61ea3f1e9ce0c5715c4bad94f4a0ef90a0.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171113112851/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/06d0/2a61ea3f1e9ce0c5715c4bad94f4a0ef90a0.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=2017-11-13|doi=10.1016/0925-8574(95)00054-2|s2cid=13068184}}</ref> {{rp|126}}

===Living Technologies Inc.===
Todd also co-founded Living Technologies Inc. (LTI), an ecological design, engineering, and construction company, in [[Burlington, Vermont]].  It was incorporated as a company on October 26, 1994, in the state of Florida.<ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|85}} Some of the personnel involved in Living Technologies, including president Michael Shaw, had  connections to OAI and to a prior company called Advanced Greenhouse Systems (AGS) which had been established in 1989 by William Rapp, also in Burlington Vermont.<ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|84–85}}  Two patents for  Ecological Fluidized Beds (EFB) were filed by John Todd and Michael Shaw in 1993 and 1995. The patents were granted to OAI in 1996 and 1997. EFBs were used in the design of what were increasingly referred to as living machines.<ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|95}}<ref name="Patent1996">{{cite web|title=Ecological fluidized bed method for the treatment of polluted water, US. Patent 5,486,291, granted January 23, 1996|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5486291|website=Google Patents|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Patent1997">{{cite web|title= Ecological fluidized bed system, US. Patent 5,618,413, granted April 8, 1997|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5618413|website=Google Patents|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref>

In 1997, Living Technologies Inc. sought a second round of funding, which it obtained from Tom Worrell. In 1998, there was considerable reorganization of the company and its board. Worrell assumed ownership of the company in 1999 and acquired the rights to the original patents for Todd's "Living Machine".  As of December 2000, in an out-of-court settlement, Worrell obtained the sole right to use "Living  Machine" as a proprietary term. Worrell's company went through a number of name changes and relocations.  Worrell Water Technologies, LLC of [[Charlottesville, Virginia]] currently holds the registered trademark for the name [[Living Machine]]. Worrell Water Technologies has redesigned Todd's original systems and patented a number of new technologies since 2002.<ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|97–101}}

===John Todd Ecological Design Inc.===
In 1989, Todd incorporated "John Todd Research and Design" in [[Falmouth, Massachusetts]]. It later became "John Todd Ecological Design" (JTED).<ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|82}}<ref name="Synapse">{{cite web|title=LIVING MACHINES by Biomimicry 3. 8 BY JOHN TODD ECOLOGICAL DESIGN|url=https://static1.squarespace.com/static/59d81f72b7411cdef9af3e92/t/5a301c038165f55070274dfc/1513102385475/JTED+Case+Study+Spreads.pdf|website=Synapse|page=22|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref>
Through this company, Todd has developed his own later-generation wastewater treatment systems, under the name "Eco-machines".
As of 2014, John Todd Ecological Design registered the trademark for the term "Eco-machines".<ref name="Eco-Machine">{{cite web|title=Eco-Machine|url=https://trademarks.justia.com/861/77/eco-86177121.html|website=Justia Trademarks|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref>
Todd's son, Jonathan Todd, is the president of John Todd Ecological Design.<ref name="Santoro">{{cite news|last1=Santoro|first1=Chrissa J.|title=Omega, BNIM Architects, and John Todd Ecological Design Celebrate Grand Opening of the Omega Center for Sustainable Living|url=https://www.eomega.org/about-omega/press-center/omega-bnim-architects-and-john-todd-ecological-design-celebrate-grand|access-date=4 May 2018|work=Omega|date=June 25, 2009}}{{Dead link|date=November 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

===University of Vermont===
Todd taught at the [[University of Vermont]] as a guest lecturer beginning in 1997. He became a research professor in 1999. He is now a research professor emeritus and distinguished lecturer.<ref name="CV"/>

==Ecological design==
Todd and his colleagues were some of the first people to actually create miniature ecosystems, largely self-perpetuating, which applied ecological principles to address human needs.<ref name="Anker">{{cite journal|last1=Anker|first1=Peder|title=The closed world of ecological architecture|journal=The Journal of Architecture|date=November 2005|volume=10|issue=5|pages=527–552|doi=10.1080/13602360500463230|s2cid=145759934}}</ref>{{rp|535}}  
Todd's approach is one of [[biomimicry]], in which a complex natural ecosystem such as a [[marsh]] is studied, recreated  and adapted.<ref name="Heerwagen">{{cite book|last1=Heerwagen|first1=Judith|last2=Mador|first2=Martin|last3=Kellert|first3=Stephen R.|title=Biophilic design the theory, science and practice of bringing buildings to life|date=2013 |publisher=Wiley|location=Hoboken, N.J.|isbn=9781118174241 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FyNer_nQrW4C&pg=PT50}}</ref>
Learning from the natural system, the ecological designer combines micro-organisms, fish, and plants into a functionally complex system<ref name="Picard"/> that is capable of carrying out tasks such as [[bioremediation]] and [[phytoremediation]].<ref name="Kangas">{{cite book|last1=Kangas|first1=Patrick C.|title=Ecological engineering : principles and practice|date=2004|publisher=Lewis|location=Boca Raton, Fla. [u.a.]|isbn=978-1566705998|pages=65, 193|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HSzKKSDYjLYC&pg=PA193}}</ref><ref name="Stephenson">{{cite journal|last1=Stephenson|first1=Chloe|last2=Black|first2=Colin R.|title=Review: One step forward, two steps back: the evolution of phytoremediation into commercial technologies|journal=Bioscience Horizons|date=2014|volume=7|doi=10.1093/biohorizons/hzu009|url=https://www.academia.edu/27970473|access-date=1 May 2018|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Todd emphasized the importance of establishing an ecosystem with a large number of diverse species and then allowing it to "settle" to a stable state, a process that could take weeks, months, or even years. He recommended seeding the ecosystem with local species, ones that had already demonstrated an ability to withstand conditions in the target environment.<ref name="Gilman"/><ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|230–232}}
He sought to create systems that were capable of self-organizing and displaying emergent properties.  Such systems are of necessity complex and cannot be well understood in terms of simple reductionism.<ref name="Daniel">{{cite web|last1=Wahl|first1=Daniel Christian|title=Design Theory and a Changing Scientific Worldview|url=https://blog.prototypr.io/design-theory-and-a-changing-scientific-worldview-6fe78e7a9393|website=Prototypr|date=May 13, 2017}}</ref>

{{blockquote|"The most interesting thing I have learned is the ability of living systems—given enough biological diversity—to self-organize, self-design, self-repair, self-replicate, and solve multiple problems for people. These include growing foods, generating fuels, cleaning up pollutants, treating sewage and other wastes, and repairing damaged environments." John Todd, 2017<ref name="Omega"/>}}

Todd has applied these ideas in various ways, to create types of applications including  "bioshelters"<ref name="Gilman"/> or  "arks", 
"ecological treatment systems" (ETS),<ref name="Dixon">{{cite journal|last1=Dixon|first1=Travis|last2=Epp|first2=Karly|last3=Munoz|first3=Santiago|last4=Porter|first4=Ryan|title=A Living Machine for Cange, Haiti. A Design and Implementation Plan|journal=Department of Environmental Science and Technology|date=10 May 2010|url=https://enst.umd.edu/sites/enst.umd.edu/files/_docs/ENST%20481%20Group%202.pdf|access-date=3 May 2018|archive-date=4 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180504012105/https://enst.umd.edu/sites/enst.umd.edu/files/_docs/ENST%20481%20Group%202.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
"advanced ecologically engineered systems" (AEES)<ref name="Wells"/>
"living machines",<ref name="EPA"/> 
and "eco-machines".<ref name="Eco-Machine"/>

===Water===
[[Image:Oberlin living machine1.JPG|right|thumb|250px|A filter tank from the [[living machines|living machine]] at [[Oberlin College]]]]

This work has resulted in innovative new approaches to processing [[wastewater]] and [[sewage]].<ref name="Milani">{{cite book|last1=Milani|first1=Brian|title=Designing the green economy : the postindustrial alternative to corporate globalization|date=1999|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|location=Lanham, MD|isbn=9780847691906|pages=[https://archive.org/details/designinggreenec0000mila/page/73 73], 104|url=https://archive.org/details/designinggreenec0000mila|url-access=registration|access-date=2 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Mongillo">{{cite book|editor-last1=Mongillo|editor-first1=John|editor-last2=Booth|editor-first2=Bibi|title=Environmental activists|date=2001|publisher=Greenwood Press|location=Westport, Conn. [u.a.]|isbn=9780313308840|pages=279–282|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n42Rf_ibaMcC&pg=PA281}}</ref>

Todd and colleagues developed what they called "[[living machines]]".  These systems are ecologically engineered technologies developed to restore, conserve, or remediate polluted water, by replicating and accelerating the natural purification processes of [[stream]]s, [[pond]]s and [[marsh]]es.  In practical application, a living machine is a self-contained treatment system designed to treat a specific waste stream using the principles of ecological engineering.  
It does this by creating diverse communities of bacteria and other microorganisms, algae, plants, trees, snails, fish and other living creatures in a series of tanks.<ref name="Lerner"/>{{rp|49–50}}   
The EPA has concluded that this approach is  appropriate to the  treatment of  municipal and some industrial  types of wastewater, and that it can be competitive in cost compared to more conventional systems.<ref name="EPA">{{cite web|title=Wastewater Technology Fact Sheet The Living Machine|url=https://www3.epa.gov/npdes/pubs/living_machine.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041117161626/http://www.epa.gov/npdes/pubs/living_machine.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 17, 2004|website=U.S. EPA|access-date=2 May 2018}}</ref>

===Sewage===
[[Greenhouse]] [[waste treatment]] plants such as the ones John Todd has developed can yield clean water from sewage. [[Bacteria]] consume the organic sewage and turn [[ammonia]] into [[nitrate]]s. The nitrates are used as food for algae and fertilizer for [[duckweed]]. [[Zooplankton]] and snails consume the [[algae]]. Fish eat the zooplankton. Floating plants soak up the leftovers. [[Schoenoplectus|Bulrush]]es, [[Typha|cattail]]s, and [[water hyacinth]]s render the toxins harmless. Trees absorb [[heavy metals]]. The byproducts are decorative plants and [[minnow]]s, both of which are sold.  The minnows are sold as bait fish. Aquatic plants, raised in the system's open-air lagoons for sewer treatment, are used in California, Florida, and Mississippi.<ref name="Lerner"/> {{rp|49–53}}
By enclosing such a system within a greenhouse, it becomes possible to do this in the colder northern climates as well.<ref name="Austin"/>{{rp|90–91}}

== Projects ==
Todd's waste treatment systems have been implemented for sites in at least nine countries, in both the industrialized and developing world.
Sites include Australia, Brazil, Canada, Czechoslovakia, England,  Hungary, India, Scotland, and the United States.<ref name="Mongillo"/>
A number of projects have been particularly noteworthy because of the introduction of new concepts or major achievements.

=== The Cape Cod Ark ===
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?time_continue=140&v=OzMUhmkI96o “Escape to a Falmouth bioshelter”], 2015, CapeCast }}

Soon after its founding in 1969, the New Alchemy Institute began to develop its first experimental environment, eventually known as the "Cape Cod Ark", at their headquarters in [[Falmouth, Massachusetts]] on [[Cape Cod]]. Their goals were to process wastewater and to explore the potential for food production.<ref name="Hugus">{{cite journal|last1=Hugus|first1=Elise|title=The Cape Cod Ark|journal=Edible Cape Cod|date=December 16, 2014 |url=http://ediblecapecod.ediblecommunities.com/food-thought/cape-cod-ark|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref>

A series of solar ponds, each with its own ecosystem, processes wastewater and uses recaptured materials to farm fish and to grow vegetables and fruits. These include papaya trees, eggplants, tomatoes, and herbs.  Computers were introduced to monitor and study the processes of remediation, energy use, and food production. Heating and electricity needs were met using renewable energy sources. The system was enclosed within a greenhouse, designed by architects Sean Wellesley-Miller and Day Chahroudi, so that it could operate year-round.<ref name="Hugus"/><ref name="Greene">{{cite web|last1=Greene|first1=Wade|title=New Alchemy Revisited APF Fellow|url=http://aliciapatterson.org/stories/new-alchemy-revisited|access-date=2 May 2018|website=Alicia Patterson Foundation|date=1978}}</ref><ref name="MEN">{{cite news|title=The New Alchemy Institute Starts Its Second Decade |work=Mother Earth News|date=January 1980 |url=https://www.motherearthnews.com/homesteading-and-livestock/new-alchemy-institute-zmaz80jfzraw|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref><ref>''Observations of Plant Response and Food Production in Solar Bioshelters''. November 1977. Kathi Ryan & Earle Barnhart. [Report on maiden winter of Cape Cod Ark, built in fall 1976 ]</ref>

When the New Alchemy Institute dissolved in 1991, the Cape Cod Ark became the property of a private co-housing community. In 1999, it was taken over by Hilde Maingay and Earle Barnhart, two of the co-founders of the New Alchemy Institute. Working with architect Ate Atema, they upgraded the structure and added an energy-efficient house to the original greenhouse. Under their care, the 1800 square feet Ark became a self-sustaining home, supporting humans, plants, fishes and animals year-round. The Cape Cod Ark was still their home as of 2021. Having provided both an experimental testbed for New Alchemy's ideas, and a sustainable home for two of its founding members for over 15 years, the Cape Cod Ark has been referred to as "New Alchemy’s crowning achievement".<ref name="Hugus"/>

=== The Prince Edward Island Ark ===
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  | video1 = [https://peiark.com/2016/10/pei-ark-video-introduction/ “The Ark for PEI: a video introduction”], October 26, 2016, [[Confederation Centre of the Arts]] }}

In 1974 Todd returned to Canada to design and build "An ARK for P.E.I." at Spry Point, Kings County on [[Prince Edward Island]], with financial support from the federal and provincial governments.<ref name="SA"/> 
Completed by David Bergmark and Ole Hammarlund of Solsearch Architects and the New Alchemy Institute, the Ark gained national attention.<ref name="Leroux">{{cite news|last1=Leroux|first1=John|title=Living Lightly on the Earth|url=https://www.canadianarchitect.com/features/review-living-lightly-earth/|access-date=2 May 2018|work=Canadian Architect|date=March 9, 2017|archive-date=3 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180503042118/https://www.canadianarchitect.com/features/review-living-lightly-earth/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="CA">{{cite news|title="Living Lightly on the Earth" explores building the ark for Prince Edward Island|url=https://www.canadianarchitect.com/architecture/ark-for-prince-edward-island/1003735501/|access-date=26 April 2018|work=Canadian Architect|date=October 17, 2016|archive-date=27 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180427045347/https://www.canadianarchitect.com/architecture/ark-for-prince-edward-island/1003735501/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Catalogue">{{cite web|title=Introduction|url=https://peiark.com/introduction/|website=The PEI Ark Catalogue|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref>
It was officially opened by Prime Minister [[Pierre Trudeau]] on September 21, 1976.<ref name="Coates">{{cite book|editor-last1=Coates|editor-first1=Colin M.|title=Canadian Countercultures and the Environment|date=2016|publisher=University of Calgary|location=Calgary, Alberta|isbn=9781552388143 |pages=153–177 |last=Trim|first=Henry|chapter=An Ark for the Future: Science, Technology, and the Canadian Back-to-the-Land Movement of the 1970s|chapter-url=https://prism.ucalgary.ca/bitstream/handle/1880/51091/CanadianCountercultures_2016_chapter07.pdf;jsessionid=9A6D2A10A93E8D30070030DEBDCB3FCF?sequence=9|access-date=2 May 2018}}</ref>

The Ark was an attempt to re-examine the relationship between people and nature.<ref name="Catalogue"/> It also gave the New Alchemists an opportunity to test their ideas in a very cold climate.<ref name="Green">{{cite web|title=Bioshelter Arks|url=https://newalchemists.net/portfolio/bioshelter-arks/|website=The Green Shelter|access-date=5 May 2018|date=2015-03-16}}</ref>
{{blockquote|"It was an integrated ecological design that was part food-producing greenhouse, part aquaculture fish farm, and part autonomous family home. The whole was wrapped in a simple, yet sophisticated, systems-based structure. Exposed mechanical and plumbing runs, a rock-filled heat sink, and early solar collector panels proudly lined the building, while the dining room overlooked the greenhouse interior through a generous clerestory. It acted as an experimental living laboratory." John Leroux, 2017<ref name="Leroux"/>}}

Differing expectations about the project caused difficulties. Because the experimental nature of the Ark had been de-emphasized, the technological problems that occurred became particularly embarrassing. Also, many Canadians expected the publicly funded installation to be viewable as a demonstration project for renewable energy and [[sustainable living]]. In contrast, the New Alchemists onsite saw it as a private research installation and tried to discourage visitors. In 1977, New Alchemists David Bergmark and Nancy Willis moved out, ending the experiment in sustainable living. The Ark was supervised for two more years by Ken MacKay, a biologist hired by the provincial government's Institute of Man and Resources (IMR), and then closed in 1981.<ref name="Coates"/>{{rp|164–165}}

Nonetheless, the Ark was an important test bed for many of the principles that were later applied to "living machines",<ref name="SA"/> as well as a number of trail-blazing and now established green or sustainable technologies: solar orientation, [[Solar thermal collector|solar collectors]], [[wind energy]], [[thermal energy storage]], and [[composting toilets]].<ref name="Exhibit"/> Historian Henry Trim emphasizes the Ark's impact on Canadian culture, helping "to introduce Canadians to renewable energy and organic foods as well as pioneering green architecture, aquaponics, and sustainable farming."<ref name="Coates"/>{{rp|164–165}}

Although it was demolished in 2000,<ref name="Mannell">{{cite journal|last1=Mannell|first1=Steven|title=The dream and lie of progress: Modern Heritage, Regionalism, and Folk Traditions in Atlantic Canada|journal=Jssac / Jséac|date=2011|volume=36|issue=1|pages=99–101 |url=http://dalspace.library.dal.ca/bitstream/handle/10222/65314/vol36_1_93_105.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref> the Ark has been called one of "Prince Edward Island’ s two most iconic works of modern architecture".<ref name="Leroux"/> In 2016, it was commemorated in the exhibit ''Living lightly on the earth: building an Ark for Prince Edward Island, 1974-76'' at the [[Confederation Centre of the Arts]] in [[Charlottetown]], P.E.I.<ref name="Leroux"/><ref name="Exhibit">{{cite web|title=Living lightly on the earth: building an Ark for Prince Edward Island, 1974-76 October 22, 2016 - April 30, 2017 |url=https://confederationcentre.com/whats-on/living-lightly-on-the-earth-building-an-ark-for-prince-edward-island-1974-76/|website=Confederation Centre of the Arts|access-date=4 May 2018}}</ref>

=== Harwich, Massachusetts ===
In 1988, the town of [[Harwich, Massachusetts]] hosted a four-month pilot of one of Todd's lagoon systems, involving 21 solar aquatic ponds and a constructed marsh. The pilot's success encouraged further involvement with Ecological Engineering Associates.<ref name="Hunt"/>{{rp|85}} For Todd, it was a "watershed moment", an important proof of concept for the ecological design approach. "After the successful first trials, I knew that it was possible to do good things in bad places; in short, to heal the planet."<ref name="Dunn">{{cite news|last1=Dunn|first1=Collin|title=The TH Interview: Dr. John Todd|url=https://www.treehugger.com/culture/the-th-interview-dr-john-todd.html|access-date=5 May 2018|work=Tree Hugger|date=November 29, 2005}}</ref>

By 1990 a full-scale project was being planned for Harwich's Flax Pond, a 15-acre site. The pond suffered from significant contamination due to [[leachates]] from a nearby [[landfill]] and [[septage]] lagoons. Oxygen levels in the water were low and [[coliform bacteria]] counts were high. Sediment deposits included high levels of [[ammonia]], up to 300 times the usual levels of [[phosphorus]], and 80 times the usual concentration of [[iron]].<ref name="Wells"/><ref name="Hildegarde"/>

A floating construction called a Pond Restorer was completed in 1992. Using a windmill and solar panels as energy sources, it drew up 100,000 gallons of water per day from the bottom of the pond. The water was sent through a series of columns involving a variety of substrates, bacterial and mineral amendments, freshwater clams, and terrestrial plants. A positive oxygen regime was restored to the bottom of the pond, and sediment depth was significantly reduced by 1995.<ref name="Wells"/><ref name="Hildegarde"/><ref name="Dixon"/>{{rp|9–10}}

In the later 1990s, the design was modified to create an "advanced ecologically engineered system" (AEES).  Large reductions in phosphorus,  ammonia, and iron occurred between 1999 and 2001.<ref name="Lerner"/>{{rp|65–66}}<ref name="Wells"/><ref name="Hildegarde">{{cite web|editor-last1=Hannum|editor-first1=Hildegarde|title=Ecological Design: Reinventing the Future, Twenty-first Annual E. F. Schumacher Lecture, October 2001|first=John|last=Todd|website=Schumacher Center for a New Economics|location=Amherst, MA|date=2001 |access-date=3 May 2018 |url=http://www.centerforneweconomics.org/publications/lectures/Todd/John/Ecological-Design}}</ref><ref name="Dixon"/>{{rp|9–10}} <ref name="Kangas"/>
Beginning in June 2001, the original structure was replaced with the first large-scale wastewater application of floating AEES Restorers. Twelve Restorers are arranged across the lagoon, in a pattern designed to promote a serpentine water flow.  The installation incorporates 25,000 plants from 25 native species to remediate waste.<ref name="Wells"/>

=== Findhorn Ecovillage, Moray, Scotland ===
[[File:FindhornLM.jpg | thumb|right | Living Machine, Findhorn Ecovillage, 2006]]
The first "Living Machine" was created at [[Findhorn Ecovillage]] in [[Moray, Scotland]] in 1995.<ref name="Laylin"/>  
For its design, John Todd drew on the work of [[Käthe Seidel]] and [[H.T. Odum]].<ref name="Laylin"/> 
The system had to accommodate wastewater from an ongoing population of about 300 residents, and a seasonally fluctuating population of as many as 10,000 visitors per year.<ref name="Mongillo"/> 
The resulting installation resembles a tropical conservatory garden.
Every organism provides food for the next step in the food chain until the cycle is complete.<ref name="Laylin"/>

As a first-generation system, the Findhorn installation has undergone numerous changes.  During its first fifteen years of operation it passed regular quality checks from the [[Scottish Environment Protection Agency]] (SEPA), and was never out of compliance.<ref name="Laylin">{{cite news|last1=Laylin|first1=Tafline|title=The Living Machine: an ecological approach to poo|url=https://theecologist.org/2010/jun/08/living-machine-ecological-approach-poo|access-date=2 May 2018|work=Ecologist|date=8 June 2010}}</ref>

=== South Burlington, Vermont ===
The Vermont Advanced Ecologically Engineered System (AEES) was one of four AEES demonstration projects created with funding from the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]. The site in Chittenden County, near [[South Burlington, Vermont]], was owned by the Massachusetts Institute for Excellence in Marine and Polymer Sciences, who received the grant. The project involved Living Technologies, Inc. as a subcontractor, and Ocean Arks International, with John Todd as [[principal investigator]].<ref name="Austin">{{cite book|last1=Austin|first1=David|title=Final report on the South Burlington, Vermont advanced ecologically engineered system (AEES) for wastewater treatment. Report to the Mass. Foundation for Excellence in Marine and Polymer Sciences, Boston.|date=2000 |publisher=Living Technologies, Inc.|url=http://www.uvm.edu/~jhtodd/SBLM_Report.pdf|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref>

Project design began in 1994. The main construction was complete by December 1995, when the introduction of biological species began. 
A steady state of operation was established by May 1996 and continued to the end of 1999.<ref name="Austin"/>
The plant was designed to treat 80,000 gallons from the city's daily wastewater output of 200,000 gallons.<ref name="Crawford">{{cite news|last1=Crawford|first1=Caroline|title=Slice of Life|url=http://www.vermontguides.com/1999/5-may/may3.htm|access-date=5 May 2018|work=Business People-Vermont|date=May 1999|archive-date=7 August 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070807012417/http://www.vermontguides.com/1999/5-may/may3.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The Vermont AEES included wetlands for the extended aeration and treatment of activated sludge, with an active microbial community as well as plants, invertebrates, and fish. One of the goals of the project was to examine the approach's usefulness in a cold climate. A greenhouse  protected the plants. The installation contained two parallel trains of treatment tanks, for experimental comparisons of treatments. During the course of the project, the operators met all but one of the original design goals, and were able to improve on the original design as a result of experimenting with the tank configurations.<ref name="Austin"/>{{rp|90–91}} <ref>{{cite web|title=South Burlington Eco-Machine|url=https://www.oceanarksint.org/portfolio/south-burlington-eco-machine/|website=Ocean Arks International|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref>
The area was used as both an experimental and an educational center, and was appreciated for its "uniquely beautiful aesthetic experience".<ref name="Austin"/>{{rp|2}}

{{blockquote|"This four year long project has demonstrated the ability of the AEES to treat municipal wastewater to tertiary standards in cold climates.  The system has been proven to have highly stable treatment performance, and has lower operating and maintenance costs than conventional small treatment systems." David Austin<ref name="Austin"/>{{rp|91}} }}

===  Adam Joseph Lewis Center for Environmental Studies ===
{{external media | width = 160px | float = right | headerimage=  [[File:Oberlin Living Machine2.jpg|210px]] | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmdsBlWwSTU “The Living Machine”], 2012, [[Oberlin College]] }}

One of Todd's Living Machines was a "vital thread" in the design of the [[Adam Joseph Lewis Center for Environmental Studies]] at [[Oberlin College]] by [[David W. Orr]] in the 1990s.
While the Living Machines's primary function was to treat wastewater, it was also intended to be a model of sustainability and ecological design for the teaching of Oberlin students. Oberlin students helped to design, install, and maintain the system.<ref name="Janas">{{cite news|last1=Janas|first1=Marci|title=NATURAL WASTEWATER TREATMENT SYSTEM "VITAL THREAD" IN OBERLIN COLLEGE'S ADAM JOSEPH LEWIS CENTER FOR ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES |url=http://www.cc.oberlin.edu/newserv/stories/living_machine_release.html|access-date=2 May 2018|work=Oberlin College Online|date=August 31, 2000}}</ref>

{{blockquote|"The Living Machine® treats wastewater using a system of engineered ecologies that include microbes, plants, snails and insects, and is designed to treat up to 2,000 gallons of the building's wastewater daily in a beautiful, garden-like atmosphere. Upon completion of a water- pressurization system, the treated wastewater will be recycled back through the building for non-potable re-use."<ref name="Janas"/>}}

Due to the complexity of the systems involved and issues in communication, a number of design oversights occurred during planning and construction.  Limitations in available space and placement of features  obstructed wetland flow, a brick wall with no functional purpose shaded some of the tanks, and some of the plants were in areas that had to be traversed by maintainers.  Such problems decreased the system's effectiveness, complicated its maintenance, and had to be addressed. Researchers also regretted that a single processing track was built, limiting their ability to establish parallel control and test conditions.<ref name="Tiruchelvam">{{cite web|last1=Tiruchelvam|first1=Varuni|title=The Context of Living Machine Wastewater Treatment Technology and Documenting its Start-up at Oberlin College|url=http://www2.oberlin.edu/faculty/petersen/ENVS316/ProjectResources/LMStartupTiruchelvamThesis2000.pdf|website=Oberlin College|date=2000}}</ref>

=== Omega Center for Sustainable Living ===
[[File:Omega Center for Sustainable Living (OCSL) at Rhinebeck, New York.jpg | thumb|right | Omega Center for Sustainable Living]]
The Omega Center for Sustainable Living (OCSL) in [[Rhinebeck, New York]], was opened on June 24, 2009. The building was designed by BNIM Architects, working with John Todd Ecological Design as the ecological architects.<ref name="Santoro"/>

Designed to be self-sustaining and carbon neutral, the building includes an Eco-machine for water reclamation.  The Eco-machine's 4,500-square-foot greenhouse and [[constructed wetland]] was designed to recycle about 5 million gallons of wastewater per year through the activity of plants, bacteria, algae, snails, and fungi.<ref name="Santoro"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Omega seeks 'living building' status|url=http://www.upi.com/Science_News/2009/07/17/Omega-seeks-living-building-status/UPI-66661247849291/tab-listen/ |publisher=[[United Press International]] |date=July 17, 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Omega Institute Turns On America's First Zero-Impact "Living Building" |url=http://www.renewableenergyworld.com/rea/partner/alteris-4286/news/article/2009/08/omega-institute-turns-on-americas-first-zero-impact-living-building |date=August 24, 2009 |publisher=[[Renewable Energy World]] }}{{Dead link|date=November 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

In 2010, the Omega Center for Sustainable Living was one of two buildings world-wide to be the first fully certified "living buildings", demonstrably achieving [[Zero-energy building|net zero energy usage]] and net zero wastewater production over a period of a year.<ref name="BNIM">{{cite news|title=Omega Center for Sustainable Living First Green Building in America to Achieve Both LEED© Platinum and Living Building Challenge|url=https://www.bnim.com/news/omega-center-sustainable-living-first-green-building-america-achieve-both-leed%C2%A9-platinum-and|access-date=4 May 2018|work=BNIM|date=October 11, 2010|archive-date=5 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180505134836/https://www.bnim.com/news/omega-center-sustainable-living-first-green-building-america-achieve-both-leed%C2%A9-platinum-and|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="WUSTL">{{cite news|title=WUSTL's Living Learning Center shares the world's first full 'Living Building' certification|url=https://source.wustl.edu/2010/10/wustls-living-learning-center-shares-the-worlds-first-full-living-building-certification/|access-date=4 May 2018|work=The Source|publisher=Washington University in St. Louis|date=October 12, 2010}}</ref>

=== George D. Aiken Center, University of Vermont ===
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage= | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Od-DrUTxWQ “UVM Eco-Machine”], 2013, [[University of Vermont]] }}

As part of the green redesign of the Aiken Center at the University of Vermont, John Todd Ecological Design, Inc. supported the creation of the Aiken Center Eco Machine between 2006 and 2012.<ref name="Watzin">{{cite web|last1=Watzin|first1=Mary C.|title=Final Report: The Green Renovation and Expansion of the Aiken Center: A Sustainable Green Building Design, Collaborative Planning Process and Long-Term Demonstration and Research Project EPA Grant Number: EM833072|url=https://cfpub.epa.gov/ncer_abstracts/index.cfm/fuseaction/display.highlight/abstract/8802/report/F|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180506104245/https://cfpub.epa.gov/ncer_abstracts/index.cfm/fuseaction/display.highlight/abstract/8802/report/F|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 6, 2018|website=United States Environmental Protection Agency|access-date=6 May 2018}}</ref> 
Much of the design work for the water treatment plant was done by Matt Beamas, one of Todd's graduate students, who presented his master's thesis on the work in 2010. In addition to treating all of the wastewater from the Aiken Center, the system provides opportunities for ongoing ecological design research at the school.<ref name="Aiken">{{cite news|title=Greening of Aiken Includes Eco-Machine™ to Treat Wastewater|url=http://greening-aiken.wikispaces.com/file/view/fallwinter0809alumnews.pdf|access-date=5 May 2018|work=The Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources News|publisher=University of Vermont|page=1|date=2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Aiken Center Eco Machine|url=http://www.uvm.edu/rsenr/enews/pdfs/AikenInterns/Aiken%20Center%20EcoMachine.pdf|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Beam">{{cite book|last1=Beam|first1=Matthew M.|title=The Design of an EcoMachine for Aiken: Engineering, Ecology, and Art|date=2010|publisher=The University of Vermont|location=Burlington, Vermont|url=http://greening-aiken.wikispaces.com/file/view/Matt+Beam+Final+Project.pdf|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref><ref name="Maclay">{{cite book|last1=Maclay|first1=William|title=The new net zero : leading-edge design and construction of homes and buildings for a renewable energy future|date=2014|publisher=Chelsea Green Publishing|isbn=9781603584487|pages=104–105}}</ref>
The wastewater system includes three separate trains, for experimental study of the system's use.<ref name="Watzin"/>
The building is considered to be "a national model for green renovation of a campus building".<ref name="Filho"/>  It has been awarded LEED Platinum certification.<ref name="Filho">{{cite book|last1=Filho|first1=Wqlter Leal|last2=Pace|first2=Paul|title=Teaching Education for Sustainable Development at University Level|date=2016|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783319329284|page=199|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rHdFDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA199}}</ref>

==Recognition==
Todd's work has inspired people working on the development of closed ecosystems for living in [[space]], as well as on Earth.<ref name="Anker"/>

Todd was profiled in ''Inventing Modern America'' (2002), published by the Lemelson-MIT Program for Invention and Innovation, in which the story of the development of his innovative ecological waste treatment systems is highlighted.<ref name="Brown">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=David E.|title=Inventing modern America : from the microwave to the mouse|date=2002|publisher=MIT Press|location=Cambridge, Mass.|pages=[https://archive.org/details/inventingmoderna00brow_0/page/148 148–153]|isbn=9780262025089|url=https://archive.org/details/inventingmoderna00brow_0/page/148}}</ref>

John Todd was the inaugural winner of the international [[Buckminster Fuller Challenge]] in 2008, for his proposal for a ''Comprehensive Design for a Carbon Neutral World: The Challenge of Appalachia''. Todd put forward a program for the reclamation of more than one million acres of damaged land, through soil remediation, forestry, and the development of renewable energy.<ref name="Underwood">{{cite web|last1=Underwood|first1=Kristin|title=Dr. John Todd Wins Buckminster Fuller Challenge Award|url=https://www.treehugger.com/corporate-responsibility/dr-john-todd-wins-buckminster-fuller-challenge-award.html|website=TreeHugger|access-date=August 19, 2008}}</ref><ref name="Makovsky">{{cite news|last1=Makovsky|first1=Paul|title=The Visionary Thinking of John Todd|url=http://www.metropolismag.com/cities/the-visionary-thinking-of-john-todd/|access-date=27 April 2018|work=Metropolis|date=July 10, 2008}}</ref>

Other awards that Todd has received include the [[Chrysler Award for Innovation in Design]] in 1994,<ref name="pubmed">{{cite journal|title=Ocean Arks International pioneers environmental systems|journal=Life Support & Biosphere Science: International Journal of Earth Space|date=1995|volume=2|issue=1|pages=43–5|pmid=11538574}}</ref> and on April 22, 1996, an [[Environmental Merit Award]] (from the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]]).<ref name="Mongillo"/><ref name="McIntyre">{{cite web|last1=McIntyre|first1=Frank|title=16 From Massachusetts Receive EPA Awards|url=https://www.epa.gov/archive/epapages/newsroom_archive/newsreleases/aa9fc8df19156d44852574fd000ab6f2.html|website=United States Environmental Protection Agency|date=April 21, 1996}}</ref>

In 1998, the Todds received the [[Bioneers]] Lifetime Achievement Award.<ref name="Hannum"/> Also in 1998 they were the first couple to receive the Lindbergh Award in recognition of their work in technology and the environment.<ref name="Lindbergh">{{cite web|title=Dr. John H. and Nancy Jack Todd 1998 Recipient|url=http://lindberghfoundation.org/john-and-nancy-jack-todd|website=Lindbergh Foundation|access-date=26 April 2018|archive-date=22 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170622085746/http://lindberghfoundation.org/john-and-nancy-jack-todd|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Lindbergh Award|url=http://lindberghfoundation.org/lindbergh-award|website=Lindbergh Foundation|access-date=26 April 2018|archive-date=5 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905100000/http://lindberghfoundation.org/lindbergh-award|url-status=dead}}</ref> They are Fellows of the [[Findhorn Foundation]].<ref name="Findhorn">{{cite web|title=Findhorn Fellows|url=https://www.findhorn.org/findhorn-fellows/|website=Findhorn Foundation|access-date=26 April 2018}}</ref> 
Todd is a fellow of the [[Gund Institute for Ecological Economics]].<ref name="Gordon">{{cite book|last1=Gordon|first1=Richard|last2=Seckbach|first2=Joseph|title=The science of algal fuels : phycology, geology, biophotonics, genomics and nanotechnology|date=2012|publisher=Springer|location=Dordrecht|isbn=9789400751095|page=448|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7DFD_MgqbRsC&pg=PA448|access-date=5 May 2018}}</ref>
